summary: This section explains the rules for issuing and managing debentures in a company. It covers conversion options, voting rights, creating reserve funds, and appointing trustees to protect investors. It also outlines what happens if a company fails to pay or redeem its debentures.
points: A company can issue debentures that convert into shares if the shareholders pass a special resolution.
Debentures can never carry any voting rights.
Companies must create a debenture redemption reserve account out of profits available for dividends, which can only be used to redeem debentures.
If a public offer or an offer to more than five hundred members is made, the company must appoint one or more debenture trustees first.
Debenture trustees must protect investor interests and fix their grievances, and they cannot be freed from liability for failing to show proper care.
The Tribunal can order a company to redeem debentures immediately if it fails to pay interest or principal on time.
example: Meera Textiles Private Limited decided to raise money by issuing debentures to the public. Because the offer was going out to many people, Meera Textiles appointed a debenture trustee beforehand to protect the investors. The company also promised to create a special reserve account out of its profits. Later, some investors worried that the company might not have enough assets to pay back the principal amount. The debenture trustee checked the situation and decided to file a petition before the Tribunal so that the Tribunal could place restrictions on the company taking on any further liabilities to keep the investors safe.

terms.meaning: A type of debt instrument issued by a company that acknowledges a loan and usually promises to pay regular interest.
A decision approved by a high majority of votes at a general meeting of the company.
A person or entity appointed to protect the rights and interests of the debenture-holders.
The repayment of the principal amount of the debentures by the company to the holders.

watch: People often confuse debentures with shares, but debentures are actually loans made to the company and do not give any voting rights.
